strengths: First work achieving logarithmic regret in KL-regularized game-theoretic settings, closing a gap from single-agent RL literature
Novel superoptimistic bonus technique elegantly exploits structure of KL-regularized best responses (Gibbs distributions), with rigorous technical analysis
Comprehensive treatment providing both regularization-dependent O(log T) and regularization-independent O(√T) bounds, enabling algorithm applicability across parameter regimes
Clean algorithmic approach using best response sampling and closed-form best response structures to avoid needing equilibrium computations
Well-motivated practical application to LLM alignment and self-play methods, timely for modern deep learning
Rigorous proofs with careful handling of multiple value/Q-function estimates and projection operators
weaknesses: Severe polynomial dependence limits practical applicability: Markov games require O(β⁻¹d³H⁷log²(dT/δ)) with H⁷ term being prohibitive (e.g., H=10 gives 10⁷ factor), suggesting analysis is not tight

Strong restrictive assumptions including exact linear function approximation, perfect realizability, and finite action spaces; no treatment of misspecification or continuous actions common in practice
Unspecified universal constants c₁, c₂ in bonus functions (Eq. 24) prevent reproducibility and practical implementation; constants only stated to be 'large enough'
Logarithmic regret advantage vanishes when β is small, contradicting the motivation that LLM alignment often requires small β for safety guarantees
Bounds ignore reference policy quality despite motivation that reference policies encode domain knowledge; stated as future work but critical for practical use
Complete absence of experiments (synthetic or real problems), making it impossible to verify the claimed log vs √T behavior or assess practical impact on even simple benchmarks

Dense 52-page presentation with key insights buried in appendix; only 2 pages of proof overview in main text; projection operator design at Π^+_h(x)=max{0,min{x,3(H-h+1)²}} appears arbitrary without justification for constant 3
Computational complexity of iterative best response and Nash equilibrium computations not discussed; numerical stability of softmax in Gibbs distribution computation not addressed
Superoptimistic gap property (Lemma C.4) heavily exploits specific projection design with unclear robustness to perturbations; sensitivity analysis absent
Unregularized Markov game rate Õ(d^{3/2}H³√T) is worse than prior OMNI-VI by factor H with no explanation, suggesting potential looseness in analysis

strengths: First work to achieve logarithmic regret in KL-regularized game-theoretic settings, closing a significant theoretical gap from √T to log T with β⁻¹ dependence

Novel algorithmic concepts: super-optimistic bonuses and best-response sampling provide creative solutions to technical challenges (e.g., handling unbounded value functions and lack of closed-form NE policies)
Technically sound with comprehensive proofs, covering important lemmas like stability under payoff perturbations (C.13) and novel covering number bounds (C.11)
Well-motivated problem addressing practical applications to LLM alignment, with clear exposition of technical challenges and how they are overcome
Results reduce correctly to known single-agent RL bounds, providing a consistency check, and extend naturally to both matrix and Markov games
weaknesses: Presentation is extremely dense and difficult to follow: main theorems mix logarithmic and √T bounds without clear guidance on when each applies; core insights are buried in technical details

High polynomial factors severely limit practical impact: d³H⁷ dependence for Markov games is substantial, and the β⁻¹ improvement only helps for small β (strong regularization), but practical interest may lie in larger β regimes
Limited scope: restricted to linear function approximation and two-player zero-sum games; extension to general function approximation (Section D.2) only sketched
No experimental validation or concrete examples: paper provides no empirical evidence that practitioners would benefit, nor guidance on problem sizes where log T improvement manifests

Dense technical choices lack intuition: e.g., projection ceiling of 3(H-h+1)² appears ad-hoc; the log(1/min{1,β}) factor in bonuses appears without clear motivation; parameter dependencies in Table 1 not clearly explained
Missing computational complexity analysis: solving KL-regularized Nash equilibrium at each step is non-trivial but not discussed; constants in O-tilde notation could be substantial

strengths: First to achieve logarithmic regret in KL-regularized game-theoretic settings, addressing an important theoretical gap
Novel superoptimistic bonus concept provides creative solution to unbounded value functions in KL-regularized games
Comprehensive treatment of both matrix and Markov games with complete theoretical analysis and proofs
Addresses timely problem motivated by LLM alignment and self-play methods
Provides both regularization-dependent and regularization-independent regret bounds
weaknesses: Prohibitive polynomial dependencies in regret bounds (d³H⁷ for Markov games)—H⁷ is indefensible without lower bounds or justification; even single-agent specialization only achieves H⁵
Complete absence of experiments: no synthetic validation of theory, no empirical investigation of β dependence, no baseline comparisons—critical weakness for ICML

Limited algorithmic novelty: uses standard optimism and best-response sampling; only superoptimistic bonus is novel, representing incremental advance over existing single-agent work (Zhao et al. 2025b)
Restrictive assumptions limiting practical applicability: linear function approximation, known reference policies, realizability, full-support assumption
Presentation issues: algorithmic insights buried, superoptimistic bonus design choices (factor of 3, factor of 2) lack intuition, theorem statements unclear about parameter dependencies
Missing analysis of tightness: no lower bounds, unclear whether H⁷ is fundamental or analytical artifact, no sensitivity analysis on β parameter
Technical concerns: extremely loose covering number bounds, log(1/min{1,β}) terms unexplained, projection operator design appears ad-hoc
Paper lacks guidance on practical usage: hyperparameter selection, computational complexity of solving KL-regularized games at each step unaddressed
No discussion of when logarithmic regime actually dominates √T regime or when algorithm is practically useful

strengths: First logarithmic regret bounds for KL-regularized game-theoretic settings, a novel and meaningful theoretical contribution that improves upon existing Õ(√T) guarantees
Well-motivated problem connected to modern LLM alignment and self-play methods; clear articulation of why reference policies (pretrained models) are valuable
Novel technical innovation: superoptimistic bonuses that exceed standard optimistic upper bounds, enabling the logarithmic regret guarantee through a cleverly designed projection operator
Elegant algorithmic approach exploiting the closed-form Gibbs distribution structure of KL-regularized best responses, sidestepping the absence of closed-form Nash equilibrium policies
Technically sound and comprehensive: complete proofs with careful auxiliary lemmas (C.1-C.13) establishing concentration, covering numbers, and problem-dependent stability bounds
Dual regret guarantees (simultaneous log(T) and √T bounds) provide flexibility across parameter regimes
Proper specialization to single-agent settings (Appendix D.1) validates theoretical framework and achieves comparable bounds to prior work
weaknesses: High polynomial dependence on problem dimensions—especially H⁷ for Markov games—with insufficient justification for tightness; unclear when the log(T) improvement justifies these polynomial factors

Superoptimistic bonus design (Eq. 23) and projection operator ceiling (3(H-h+1)²) appear somewhat ad-hoc; intuition for why exactly 2× MSE bonus and 3× ceiling are necessary could be clearer in main text

Limited guidance on practical parameter selection: β⁻¹ scaling means weak regularization severely hurts performance; no explicit analysis of regimes where log(T) beats √T or concrete crossover examples
No empirical validation of theoretical predictions; given high polynomial factors, even simple synthetic experiments would strengthen confidence in practical relevance
Dense technical presentation that relegates key insights (Lemmas C.3-C.4 on optimism/superoptimism) to appendix; high-level intuitions difficult to extract
Covering number analysis (Lemmas C.10-C.11) is involved; dependence on log(1/min{1,β}) and splitting δ-budget across horizon introduce multiple log factors whose cumulative effect deserves discussion
Incomplete comparison with prior work: Yang et al. [2025a] achieves Õ(dH^{3/2}√T), but explicit analysis of when SOMG's Õ(β^{-1}d³H⁷ log²(T)) is preferable is missing
